# Model card: XGBoost labour-market forecaster (`xgboost_v1`)

*Generated by `src/training/make_model_card.py` from the files in this folder and in `reports/training/`; do not edit by hand.*

## 1. Summary

Three gradient-boosted tree models (XGBoost 3.4.1), one for each of employed workers (E), job vacancies (V) and registered seekers (S), forecast the log change of a district-sector series 1 to 12 months ahead. Each model is a mean of 5 random-seed fits. The models were trained on the train split only (target months 2014-02-01 to 2022-02-01, 307,440 rows), checked on a separate validation split (2022-03 to 2022-12, 15,400 rows), and never saw the test split. This card describes the Phase 7 deliverable; the final test evaluation is Phase 8.

| Target | Validation WAPE % | Same rows: last value + seasonal shift | Improvement | Phase 6 default settings, same pipeline |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| employed workers (E) | 4.19 | 4.98 | 16% | 4.08 |
| job vacancies (V) | 8.56 | 9.43 | 9% | 8.49 |
| registered seekers (S) | 9.54 | 21.19 | 55% | 9.54 |

WAPE = sum of absolute count errors / sum of actual counts, averaged with equal weight over the horizons present in validation (1 to 10). Seekers are scored without excluding any month; their validation window lies inside the e-Shram registration ramp (see Section 9).

## 2. Intended use and limits

* **Use:** monthly district-sector forecasts of employment, vacancies and registered seekers for the labour-market dashboard and the skill demand-supply gap (SIH26246), after the Phase 8 test evaluation and sign-off.
* **Not for:** decisions about individuals, districts or sectors outside the 56 districts x 5 sectors, or horizons beyond 12 months. The data are synthetic (generated to mimic official statistics), so accuracy here says how well the method works on this simulator, not on real data.
* **No real forecasts yet:** this phase produces and validates the model; no forecast has been published.

## 3. Data and splits

Source: `data/processed/panel_monthly.parquet` (56 districts x 5 sectors = 280 series x 192 months, 2011-01 to 2026-12). The file `data/splits/{train,validation,test}.parquet` (built by `src/splits/make_splits.py`, checksums in `data/splits/split_manifest.json`) holds one row per series, forecast origin and horizon.

| Split | Calendar window | Months | Share of calendar | Rows | Origin rule |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| train | 2011-01 to 2022-02 | 134 | 69.8% | 307,440 | origin on or after 2014-01 (36 months of history), so train targets run from 2014-02 |
| validation | 2022-03 to 2022-12 | 10 | 5.2% | 15,400 | origin on or after the last train month, so the longest horizon is 10 |
| test (locked) | 2023-01 to 2026-12 | 48 | 25.0% | 142,800 | origin on or after the last validation month; not read in this phase |

* **Time-aware, not random.** The autocorrelated series are split into consecutive blocks of calendar time with the same cut dates for every series. A random or per-row stratified split would put neighbouring months in different splits and leak the future into training.
* **Balanced by sector by construction.** Every sector has 56 series and therefore the same 134 / 10 / 48 months and the same number of rows in each split (checked in `tests/test_splits.py`). Rows are assigned by target month, so the three files have disjoint targets in time order; 36,680 rows that straddle a boundary without satisfying the origin rule are dropped.
* **Independent files.** The train and validation files can be rebuilt exactly from a panel that stops at the end of their window (`tests/test_splits.py`). Features of a validation row may look back into the train period (that is history, known at the forecast origin), never forward.
* **Shock handling.** Employed-worker training rows whose window (12 months before the origin to the target month) touches COVID (2020-03 to 2022-02) or the 2016-17 policy spans are removed (124,320 of the 307,440 train rows remain for E). Vacancy and seeker models train on all rows (Phase 5 policy). Scoring excludes target months inside those shocks for E and V; the validation window (2022-03 on) is clear of them. Seekers are scored on all months.
* **Phase 5/6 exposure.** Features, base choices and the model family were selected in Phases 5-6 with folds that used 2018, 2019 and 2024 as validation years. The new test window (2023-2026) therefore contains 2023 and 2024 months that influenced those choices, and 2025-26 was scored once by the quarantined prototype. Phase 8 must say so.

## 4. Model architecture

* **Family:** gradient-boosted decision trees (XGBoost `XGBRegressor`, `tree_method='hist'`, leaf-wise growth). Chosen in Phase 6 (tied with scikit-learn HistGradientBoosting; 0.59 points better than the best baseline pooled).
* **One global model per target** (E, V, S) across all 280 series. **Direct multi-horizon:** the horizon (1-12) is an input feature, so one model answers every horizon; no recursive forecasting.
* **Prediction target:** the log change `log(value at t+h) - log(base at t)`, with base = last value (E), mean of the last 3 months (V) or last 6 months (S) (Phase 5 choice). Predicted count = exp(base + predicted change).
* **Ensemble:** the saved model for each target is the mean of the predicted changes of 5 XGBoost models trained with seeds [42, 43, 44, 45, 46] (they differ in row and feature sampling). One fit moves by 1.0-1.7% of its validation WAPE across seeds (Section 7); averaging removes most of that.
* **Lag and rolling features** (all trailing, built only from months at or before the forecast origin; verified by a truncation test in `tests/test_features.py`): momentum = log change over the last 1, 3, 6, 12 and 36 months; deviation of the current level from its 3-, 6- and 12-month rolling means; 12-month rolling volatility of monthly changes; sector-wide aggregates of the same quantities; a trailing seasonal profile and the seasonal change expected between the origin month and the target month; the value one year before the target; calendar month of origin and target.

| Target | Features | Base | Shock windows removed from training |
|---|---|---|---|
| employed workers (E) | 36 | last | yes |
| job vacancies (V) | 29 | sm3 | no |
| registered seekers (S) | 68 | sm6 | no |

## 5. Preprocessing (fitted on the train split only)

`src/training/preprocess.py`, stored in `preprocessor.json`. `fit` refuses any rows that are not labelled `train`; validation, test and new data are only transformed (`tests/test_training.py`).
1. **Missing values:** replaced by the training median of each feature. The train split has 0 missing values (the 36-month history requirement removes them), so this is a safeguard for new data.
2. **Scaling:** continuous features are standardised with the training mean and standard deviation; horizon and calendar codes are left as they are.
3. **Effect on this model:** none that matters. Trees split on thresholds, so scaling does not change what they can learn. Refitting without preprocessing changes validation WAPE by +0.020 points for E, +0.000 for V and +0.000 for S (`reports/training/preprocessing_check.json`). The step is kept because it was required, it costs nothing, and the same pipeline can feed linear or neural challengers.

## 6. Hyper-parameters and how they were chosen

### 6.1 Final values

| Parameter | E | V | S | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `objective` | reg:squarederror | reg:squarederror | reg:squarederror | Loss function. Squared error on the log change; large errors are not down-weighted |
| `tree_method` | hist | hist | hist | Histogram split finding (multi-core) |
| `grow_policy` | lossguide | lossguide | lossguide | Leaf-wise growth: always split the leaf with the largest gain, up to max_leaves |
| `max_depth` | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 = no depth limit; complexity is limited by max_leaves instead |
| `max_leaves` | 63 | 63 | 31 | Leaves per tree. Fewer leaves = smoother, more regularised trees |
| `learning_rate` | 0.03 | 0.08 | 0.08 | Shrinkage applied to each tree's contribution |
| `n_estimators` | 300 | 40 | 250 | Number of trees (chosen by the cross-validation checkpoints, see Section 6) |
| `min_child_weight` | 800 | 200 | 100 | Minimum summed Hessian in a leaf = minimum number of training rows in a leaf for squared error |
| `reg_lambda` | 20 | 50 | 5 | L2 penalty on leaf values |
| `reg_alpha` | 0 | 0.1 | 0 | L1 penalty on leaf values |
| `gamma` | 0.001 | 0.001 | 0 | Minimum loss reduction needed to make a split (on the squared-error scale of the log change) |
| `subsample` | 0.9 | 0.7 | 0.8 | Fraction of rows sampled for each tree |
| `colsample_bytree` | 0.8 | 1 | 0.8 | Fraction of features sampled for each tree |
| `colsample_bynode` | 0.8 | 0.8 | 1 | Fraction of features sampled at each split |
| `max_bin` | 256 | 256 | 256 | Histogram bins per feature |
| `n_jobs` | -1 | -1 | -1 | CPU threads (-1 = all cores) |
| `verbosity` | 0 | 0 | 0 | Silent |

Seeds of the five-model ensemble: [42, 43, 44, 45, 46] (`random_state` above is the base value; each ensemble member overrides it). The Phase 6 default was: learning rate 0.08, 250 trees, 31 leaves, min_child_weight 100, lambda 5, alpha 0, gamma 0, subsample 0.8, colsample_bytree 0.8, 256 bins.

### 6.2 Regularisation methods in use

* **Shrinkage and early stopping of the tree count:** a low learning rate and a tree count chosen at the best cross-validation checkpoint, not the maximum.
* **Leaf-size limits:** `max_leaves` and `min_child_weight` (at least that many rows per leaf) stop trees fitting single districts.
* **Penalties:** `reg_lambda` (L2) shrinks leaf values; `reg_alpha` (L1) and `gamma` (minimum split gain) were searched and are kept only where the search chose them (E uses only a tiny gamma, V a small alpha and gamma, S none).
* **Stochastic sampling:** `subsample`, `colsample_bytree` and `colsample_bynode` give each tree a different view of rows and features.
* **Seed averaging:** five models per target.
* **Data-side:** shock windows removed from E training; time-ordered folds only; detrended features (time-proxy features were excluded in Phase 5).

### 6.3 Search procedure (iterative)

**Validation scheme.** Rolling-origin (expanding window) folds inside the train split: train on targets up to 2016-12 and score the next 12 target months (origins on or after the cut-off), then the same for cut-offs 2017-12 and 2018-12. Score = WAPE on counts, equal weight for horizons 1-12. Preprocessing is refitted on every fold's training rows.

| Searched parameter | Values tried |
|---|---|
| learning_rate | 0.01, 0.02, 0.03, 0.05, 0.08 |
| max_leaves | 7, 15, 31, 63 |
| min_child_weight | 50, 100, 200, 400, 800 |
| reg_lambda | 1, 5, 20, 50, 200 |
| reg_alpha | 0, 0.01, 0.1, 1 |
| gamma | 0, 0.001, 0.01, 0.05 |
| subsample | 0.5, 0.7, 0.9 |
| colsample_bytree | 0.4, 0.6, 0.8, 1 |
| colsample_bynode | 0.6, 0.8, 1 |
| max_bin | 64, 128, 256 |

| Target | CV WAPE, Phase 6 default | CV WAPE, best of search | Trials | Final choice | Its CV WAPE | Validation WAPE of the saved checkpoint | Four-fold score (default = 1) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| employed workers (E) | 1.694 (150 trees) | 1.659 (trial 46) | 59 | trial 56 | 1.667 | 4.191 | 0.995 |
| job vacancies (V) | 7.328 (40 trees) | 7.306 (trial 42) | 59 | trial 6 | 7.308 | 8.557 | 0.987 |
| registered seekers (S) | 8.024 (150 trees) | 7.769 (trial 52) | 59 | phase 6 default, 250 trees | 7.897 | 9.544 | 1.000 |

1. **Stage 1, search on the three rolling-origin folds:** the Phase 6 default plus 40 random configurations, then 18 local variations around the three best (one seed each). Gains over the default were small: E 2.1%, V 0.3%, S 3.2% better cross-validation WAPE.
2. **Stage 1 shortlist:** configurations within 1% of the best were refitted on the whole train split and scored on validation. A single fit moved by 1-2% between seeds and also between thread counts (Section 7), which is larger than the gaps between shortlisted configurations, so these were scored as five-seed averages.
3. **Stage 2, add the most recent era:** the folds above are all calm pre-COVID years. Scoring the Phase 6 default on validation showed it beating the stage-1 pick for seekers by a wide margin (11.28 vs 9.54) and slightly for E (4.20 vs 4.08), with V level. Stage 2 therefore treats the validation split as a fourth, most recent fold: the 12 best configurations by cross-validation and the default (at its cross-validated and at its Phase 6 tree count) are scored on all four folds, each fold's WAPE is divided by the default's WAPE on that fold, and the average of the four ratios decides. For E and V the winner is a tuned configuration, by 0.5% and 1.3% over the default (inside the noise); for S the default is not beaten, so it is kept. Stage-2 validation scores are 3-seed averages and differ from the saved 5-seed checkpoints by up to 0.16 points, which is the noise level.

Because validation was used in the last stage, its scores in this card are slightly optimistic. The test split in Phase 8 is the unbiased check. Full trial tables: `reports/training/tune_<E|V|S>_trials.csv`; stage-2 candidates: `tune_<E|V|S>_best.json`.

## 7. Training procedure and reproducibility

* `python src/training/train.py` reads `reports/training/tune_<k>_best.json`, verifies the split checksums, fits the preprocessor on the train rows, trains 5 seeds per target with all CPU cores, saves `<k>_seed<n>.ubj` (XGBoost native format, readable by later XGBoost versions), `preprocessor.json`, `params.json`, `intervals.json`, `checkpoint_manifest.json` (SHA-256 of every file, library versions, split checksums) and `logs/train.log`. Training took 338 s.
* **Run-to-run variation.** XGBoost's histogram trees are not bit-identical across seeds or thread counts. Single-fit validation WAPE across 8 seeds: E 4.14 to 4.28; V 8.40 to 8.77; S 9.54 to 10.07. The saved checkpoint is the reference; retraining reproduces it closely, not exactly. Loading the checkpoint is exact (`tests/test_training.py` reloads it and reproduces the saved validation predictions).
* **Learning curves** (seed 42, `learning_curves.json`): validation RMSE of the log change is lowest at 79 of 300 trees for E, 36 of 40 trees for V, 174 of 250 trees for S; the difference to the final tree is at most 1.4%, so there is no sign of late overfitting.

## 8. How to run the saved model

```python
import sys; sys.path.insert(0, 'src/training')
from predict import Forecaster
fc = Forecaster.load('models/xgboost_v1')
out = fc.predict(frame)   # frame: rows in the data/splits layout
```
```bash
python src/training/predict.py --split validation --out forecasts_validation.parquet
python src/training/predict.py --input my_rows.parquet --out my_forecasts.parquet
```
Input columns: the features listed in `params.json` plus the base columns `last_E`, `sm3_V`, `sm6_S` and `horizon`. Output per target: `pred_<k>` (count), `lo90_<k>`, `hi90_<k>`, `pred_log_<k>`. Requirements: Python 3.13, `xgboost==3.4.1`, `numpy==2.1.3`, `pandas==2.2.3`, `pyarrow` (see `requirements.txt`). The test split is refused unless `--unlock-test` is given (Phase 8). Producing features for a new origin beyond the data is a Phase 9 (deployment) task.

Rebuild from scratch: `python src/splits/make_splits.py`, then `python src/training/tune.py E|V|S`, `... --final-only`, `... --recent`, then `python src/training/train.py`, `check_preprocessing.py`, `compare_default.py`, `seed_noise.py`, `make_model_card.py`.

Validation rows: E 15,400, V 15,400, S 15,400. Origins 2022-02 to 2022-11, horizons 1 to 10 (1 to 10 only, because the 10-month window ends before a 12-month horizon fits; horizons 11-12 are untested here).

### 9.3 90% prediction intervals

Intervals are the model's predicted log level plus the 5% and 95% quantiles of its out-of-sample log errors in the three rolling-origin folds, by target and horizon (`intervals.json`). Coverage on the validation split: E 61%, V 83%, S 79% against a nominal 90%. The intervals are too narrow for this window because errors in the post-COVID recovery are larger than in 2016-2019. They need recalibration (for example on a recent rolling window) before use; this is carried to Phase 8.

## 10. Known weaknesses and open items

* **Regime shift in validation.** The validation window is the first ten months after COVID's end. Errors are about three times the in-sample errors for employed workers (4.2% vs 1.5%), partly because employment grew much faster over the forecast horizon in this window (mean log change 0.039, against 0.013 in the E training rows). The baseline suffers the same way, and the model still beats it on average, but validation accuracy is not a forecast of test accuracy.
* **Where the baseline wins** (model error above the last-value-plus-seasonal-shift error), by horizon in months: E: 1, 2, 3; V: none; S: none. The model is the better choice at longer horizons and for seekers.
* **Seekers and the e-Shram ramp.** The whole validation window is inside the registry ramp (2021-08 to 2023-02), so seeker scores here mix model skill with a one-off structural change. The seasonal-naive-plus-drift baseline, which tracks year-on-year growth, scores 10.8% against the model's 9.5%: the margin over a simple baseline is only 12%, against 55% over last value plus seasonal shift. The Phase 6 concern that seekers beyond about 9 months lose to a simple baseline (D4) is **not resolved** and needs the post-ramp test months.
* **Horizons 11-12** have no validation rows; they are covered only by the rolling-origin folds.
* **Ten months of validation and fit-to-fit variation of 1-2%** mean that differences under about 2% between settings are ties. Tuning improved cross-validation by at most a few percent and did not beat the Phase 6 default on the most recent era for seekers.
* **Intervals** under-cover (Section 9.3). **IT-ITeS vacancies and low-volume series** still need separate reporting (D5). Phase 1 accuracy thresholds are revisited in Phase 8.
* **Trees cannot extrapolate** beyond the range of changes seen in training (for example a new structural break).
